overview: The imported record starts in 1945, when this area was under French rule. Upper Volta had been dissolved as a separate colony in 1932 and was restored in 1947, so the 1945 outline is not evidence of an independent Burkina Faso. Independence followed in 1960; the present name dates to 1984.

periods.title: Colonial rule and territorial restoration
periods.summary: Upper Volta regained separate territorial status in 1947.

periods.title: Independent Upper Volta
periods.summary: Independence came in 1960, under the name Upper Volta.

periods.title: Burkina Faso
periods.summary: The country took its new name in 1984; later coups changed governments, not the existence of its people.

items.text: Upper Volta became independent on 5 August 1960. Its name referred to the river system; in 1984 it became Burkina Faso. The change belonged to Thomas Sankara’s revolutionary government, which had taken power the previous year.

A dated French writing sample survives in the legislature’s report of 29 October 2024: “Unité-Progrès-Justice,” meaning “Unity-Progress-Justice.” The report quotes this as the former motto while approving its replacement. Words on official documents can change with politics, just as flags and country names do.

Sankara was killed in the October 1987 coup that brought Blaise Compaoré to power. Much later, two coups in 2022 removed first the elected president Roch Kaboré, then the military leader Paul-Henri Damiba. These are changes of regime within a continuing country.

Francis Kéré’s first building, Gando Primary School, was completed in his home community in 2001. It tackled the practical problems of dark, overheated classrooms using locally available clay mixed with cement for stronger bricks, with an overhanging roof protecting the walls from rain.

At Gando, the metal roof sits above a separate brick ceiling. Air enters through windows and warm air escapes through openings overhead. The building does some of the cooling work itself: a lesson in engineering before the teacher has even written on the board.

Community members helped build the school, combining familiar construction skills with the architect’s engineering. Kéré’s account emphasizes methods that could also simplify future maintenance. A school building needs people who can repair it, as well as people who can design it.

At the living royal court of Tiébélé, Kasena house shapes have social meanings. Figure-of-eight mother houses accommodate elderly residents, widows, unmarried women and children; young married people occupy rectangular houses, and adolescent or unmarried men circular ones. UNESCO documented this arrangement when the site was inscribed in 2024.

Tiébélé’s buildings use earth, wood, straw and cow dung. Men construct the houses, while women preserve and teach the knowledge of symbolic wall decoration. Older motifs coexist with new ones, learned through observation and practice: these walls belong to an active community, not an abandoned stage set.

Farmer Yacouba Sawadogo improved traditional zaï planting pits after the droughts around 1980. Compost goes into the pits before seeds; rows of stones slow rainwater running away. He also put water pots in trees for birds that could bring seeds. Small holes helped produce very large changes.

From 1984, Sawadogo organized seed-sharing gatherings. Farmers brought crop samples after harvest; seeds were stored at his homestead, then selected before the rains. This was experimentation shared across villages, with the next season’s meals depending on the results.

Ouagadougou hosts FESPACO, a festival of African cinema and television. Its 2021 edition ran in October after the pandemic forced a delay. Film selection and screenings made the capital a meeting place for storytellers across borders, adding a different kind of public gathering to markets and ceremonies.

In Dori in 2024, teenager Djeneba Dicko described how a nearby water point reduced the exhausting search for water for her family. UNICEF reported eight solar-powered supply systems. Displaced resident Nafissa Sanou managed one at Petit Paris, cleaning the collection area and reminding users about hygiene.

ending.text: Burkina Faso continues as a state despite repeated changes of government and armed conflict. The two coups of 2022 ended particular governments; they did not end the country’s communities, farms, schools or cultural institutions.
